body:
What defines a Hindu temple?

A Hindu temple is a sacred building organised around the garbhagriha, the chamber containing the principal image or symbol of the deity. The word garbhagriha means womb-chamber. Its religious importance explains why the principal tower of a developed temple generally rises above this chamber rather than above the entrance hall.

Early structural temples were often small, with a sanctum and a simple porch. From about the 5th century CE, temple architecture developed increasingly elaborate towers, pillared halls, platforms and subsidiary shrines. These elements were combined in different ways across regions.

The same basic purpose could be expressed through different construction methods. A structural temple is assembled from building materials such as stone or brick. A rock-cut temple is excavated from existing rock. A monolithic temple is carved from a single mass of rock. The construction method does not, by itself, determine whether the architectural style is Nagara or Dravida.

Reading a temple through its plan

A plan represents the arrangement of spaces as viewed from above. It helps identify the sanctum, halls, entrance and possible subsidiary shrines. The main parts are:

  • Garbhagriha: The innermost sacred chamber that houses the principal image or symbol of worship.
  • Antarala: A vestibule or transitional space connecting the sanctum with a hall in temples that possess one.
  • Mandapa: A pillared hall or pavilion where worshippers may assemble. Larger temples can contain several halls.
  • Ardhamandapa: An entrance porch or smaller hall preceding the principal mandapa.
  • Mahamandapa: A larger assembly hall found in some developed temple plans.
  • Pradakshinapatha: A passage for circumambulation around the sanctum, when such a passage is provided.

These parts are not compulsory components of every temple. A small early shrine may contain only a sanctum and porch, whereas a large medieval temple may have several mandapas, courtyards and subsidiary shrines.

Reading a temple through its elevation

An elevation shows the building's vertical form. It is especially useful for distinguishing temple styles because their towers differ in shape.

  • Jagati: A raised platform on which a temple may stand.
  • Adhisthana: The architectural base or moulded foundation immediately supporting the temple walls.
  • Jangha: The main wall portion rising above the base.
  • Shikhara: Commonly the tower over the sanctum in North Indian architectural terminology.
  • Vimana: In South Indian temple descriptions, the shrine and its superstructure; the term is frequently used for the stepped tower above the sanctum.
  • Amalaka: A ribbed, disc-like crowning member associated with many Nagara towers.
  • Kalasha: A pot-shaped finial commonly placed above the crowning member.

A temple may also have a dhvajastambha, or ceremonial flagstaff, and an image of the deity's vahana, or vehicle, placed along the principal axis. Their arrangement helps explain how architecture directs attention towards the sanctum.

Why plan and elevation must be studied together

The same plan can support different tower forms. Conversely, buildings with similar-looking towers can have different arrangements of halls, enclosures and subsidiary shrines. Therefore, identifying a style requires several clues rather than reliance on a single feature.

For example, a temple with a curved sanctum tower and a lower pillared hall suggests a Nagara arrangement. A temple with a stepped pyramidal sanctum tower, enclosing walls and a monumental gateway suggests a Dravida arrangement. These are general tendencies, not rules without exceptions.

Plan describes arrangement; elevation describes height and vertical form. The garbhagriha is the sacred chamber, the mandapa is a hall, and the tower normally rises above the sanctum.

Prelims focus

  • Garbhagriha: chamber housing the principal deity.
  • Mandapa: pillared assembly hall.
  • Antarala: vestibule between the sanctum and hall.
  • Jagati: raised platform; adhisthana: architectural base.
  • Shikhara and vimana are terms whose precise usage depends on architectural tradition.
  • Trap: A monolithic temple is identified by how it was carved, not automatically by a particular regional style.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, printed pp. 123–125; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 69–71, 81–82.]

title: Understanding Temple Architecture: Plan, Elevation and Essential Parts

body:
The defining character of Nagara architecture

Nagara is the principal North Indian order of temple architecture. Its best-known feature is the tower rising above the garbhagriha. In a common Nagara form, the tower rises from a broadly square base and curves inwards as it approaches the summit.

Many Nagara temples stand on a raised stone platform approached by steps. Elaborate enclosure walls and monumental entrance gateways are generally less prominent than in the developed Dravida tradition. However, North Indian temples vary considerably across periods and regions, so these characteristics should be treated as patterns rather than universal requirements.

The tallest tower normally marks the principal sanctum. In developed examples, smaller towers may be grouped around the central shikhara, creating an upward movement towards its summit.

Three important Nagara roof and tower forms

The shape of the superstructure is especially useful for identifying a Nagara subtype.

FormShapeTypical use or clue
Latina or rekha-prasadaTall tower with walls curving or sloping inward above a broadly square baseCommon form over the main sanctum
PhamsanaBroader, lower roof with successive slabs rising on comparatively straight slopesFrequently used above mandapas
ValabhiElongated rectangular structure with a barrel-shaped or wagon-vaulted roofDistinguished by its vaulted roof rather than a high curving tower

The difference between latina and phamsana is not simply one of height. Latina is recognised by a high, continuously rising sanctum tower. Phamsana has a relatively low roof built through successive rising slabs. A temple may use both: a latina tower over the garbhagriha and a phamsana roof over the mandapa.

Valabhi is different from both because its roof resembles the rounded upper form of a covered wagon. It reflects the survival and adaptation of older architectural roof types.

Early development: the Vishnu temple at Deogarh

Some of the earliest surviving structural temples belong to the Gupta period. Small shrines at Sanchi and Udayagiri illustrate how a sanctum and modest pillared porch could form the nucleus of a temple.

The Vishnu temple at Deogarh, in present-day Uttar Pradesh, is a major early example of Nagara architecture, generally dated to the early 6th century CE. It is commonly called the Dashavatara Temple. Its developing curvilinear tower represents an important step beyond the simpler shrines of the earlier Gupta period.

Deogarh is also associated with the panchayatana arrangement. In this plan, 1 principal shrine is accompanied by 4 smaller corner shrines, making 5 shrines in all.

The surviving temple has major Vishnu reliefs, including Sheshashayana, Nara-Narayana and Gajendramoksha. Although the temple is popularly called Dashavatara, the original dedication of its 4 corner shrines is not securely known. It is therefore incorrect to assume that each corner shrine necessarily housed a particular incarnation of Vishnu.

Regional variation within northern architecture

The Nagara order was not identical throughout northern India. Central Indian temples developed increasingly elaborate clusters of towers. Odisha developed its own Kalinga vocabulary of deuls and assembly halls. Gujarat and Rajasthan developed the richly carved Maru-Gurjara tradition.

Other regions also adapted temple forms to local conditions. In Bengal, curved roof forms derived from traditional buildings influenced later brick and terracotta temples. In the western Himalayan region, some temples combined a Nagara-type sanctum tower with pitched roofs influenced by local timber construction. These are regional adaptations rather than evidence that every northern temple followed one rigid design.

Prelims focus

  • Nagara is the principal North Indian temple order.
  • Latina or rekha-prasada: tall, generally curving sanctum tower.
  • Phamsana: lower, broader roof often used for a mandapa.
  • Valabhi: rectangular building with a wagon-vaulted roof.
  • Panchayatana: 1 main shrine and 4 corner shrines.
  • Trap: Nagara does not mean every roof in the temple must be curvilinear.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 69–75, 77–81.]

title: Nagara Architecture: Northern Temple Towers and Their Main Forms

body:
Chandela patronage and temple development

The temples of Khajuraho in present-day Madhya Pradesh are outstanding examples of developed Nagara architecture. Most of the celebrated temples were constructed under the Chandela rulers during the 10th and 11th centuries CE.

Khajuraho illustrates how a relatively simple sanctum-and-hall arrangement could develop into an elaborate architectural composition. Its temples combine elevated platforms, successive halls, carefully organised wall projections and soaring towers. Most of the major surviving temples are built from finely worked sandstone.

How the towers produce a distinctive appearance

The characteristic feature of a mature Khajuraho temple is the relationship between the principal shikhara and the surrounding smaller towers. The tallest shikhara rises above the garbhagriha. Lower towers and roof forms accompany the halls and subsidiary architectural projections, creating a gradual increase in height towards the sanctum.

The result resembles a group of mountain peaks, with the principal summit dominating the composition. This effect is achieved by combining structural parts of different heights rather than simply making every part of the temple equally tall.

Many towers terminate in an amalaka, the ribbed disc-like member, and a kalasha, the pot-shaped finial above it. These are especially useful identifying features in photographs and architectural diagrams.

Principal temples and their dedications

TempleDedicationImportant association
Lakshmana TempleVishnuBuilt under Chandela ruler Yashovarman, around 954 CE; notable panchayatana plan
Kandariya Mahadeva TempleShiva11th-century Chandela temple; major example of clustered Nagara shikharas
Vishvanatha TempleShivaAnother important Chandela temple within the Khajuraho group

The Lakshmana Temple is a particularly useful example because it joins 2 ideas: a developed Nagara elevation and the panchayatana plan. Its principal shrine stands on a high platform with smaller shrines at the corners. The Archaeological Survey of India associates its construction with Yashovarman, rather than his successor Dhanga.

The Kandariya Mahadeva Temple is dedicated to Shiva. Its clustered tower composition is one of the clearest examples of the fully developed Nagara form. Both the principal shikhara and its subordinate architectural elements contribute to the impression of increasing height.

Halls, sculpture and religious diversity

A developed Khajuraho plan commonly leads from an entrance porch into successive mandapas, through an antarala and finally to the garbhagriha. Its walls contain projections and recessed surfaces that provide space for sculpture.

Khajuraho is known for extensive sculptural decoration. The carvings include divine images, attendants, musicians, ordinary activities, couples and other aspects of human life. Its erotic figures are only one part of a much wider decorative programme. They should not be treated as the defining feature of every sculpture or every temple at the site.

The surviving group includes both Hindu and Jain temples. Therefore, Khajuraho is not exclusively a Shaiva or exclusively a Hindu temple complex. The architectural style is broader than the religious dedication of any single shrine.

Distinguish the temples: Lakshmana is dedicated to Vishnu, whereas Kandariya Mahadeva is dedicated to Shiva. Both belong to the Chandela architectural tradition at Khajuraho.

Prelims focus

  • Khajuraho is in Madhya Pradesh and is associated with the Chandela dynasty.
  • Its major temples represent mature Nagara architecture.
  • Lakshmana Temple: Vishnu; associated with Yashovarman and approximately 954 CE.
  • Kandariya Mahadeva Temple: Shiva; celebrated for clustered shikharas.
  • The temple group includes Hindu and Jain monuments.
  • Trap: Do not match the Lakshmana Temple with Shiva or the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple with Vishnu.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 73–75; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, printed p. 62; Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Temples, Khajuraho, sections on Chandela monuments and Lakshmana Temple (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Khajuraho Group of Monuments, Outstanding Universal Value (consulted 23 November 2026).]
